dryRun.title: Typing "re" while a 2,000-item list re-renders
rows: list render blocks the main thread
dryRun.note: Concurrent rendering (React 18+) lets React prepare a new UI in the background, pause it for urgent work, and throw away outdated work. It is opt-in per update: urgent updates stay synchronous; transitions and deferred values become interruptible.

think.q:
function App() {
  const [tab, setTab] = useState('a')
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  return <><button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setTab('b'))}>b</button><p>{tab}{isPending ? ' (pending)' : ''}</p></>
}
why: After the transition finishes, the new tab shows and isPending is false again.

think.q: Is all rendering concurrent once you use React 18+?
opts: No, only updates marked as transitions (or deferred values, Suspense) use it
why: createRoot enables the capability; you opt in per update.

think.q: What can be interrupted?
opts: A transition render in progress, when a more urgent update arrives
why: Commits stay atomic.

think.q: What is "tearing" in concurrent rendering?
opts: Different parts of the UI showing different versions of external data during one render
why: useSyncExternalStore exists to prevent it for external stores.

think.q: What does concurrency NOT fix?
opts: Slow typing during big list updates
A single component whose render itself takes 500 ms
Showing old UI while new data loads
why: It schedules work; it cannot make one slow function fast.

try.task: Write Tabs({ tabs }) (tabs = [{ id, label, render }]) where switching tabs uses startTransition (from useTransition), the active tab button has aria-pressed="true", and the content area gets aria-busy="true" while a switch is pending.
examples: click B → aria-pressed moves, content becomes B
try.hint: const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); onClick={() => startTransition(() => setActive(id))}.

checks.t: not busy once the switch is done

takeaway.key: Concurrent rendering is opt-in per update: urgent updates stay instant, transitions can be interrupted and restarted. It schedules work; it does not speed up slow components.
mistakes: Expecting concurrency to fix a slow render.
Wrapping urgent input updates in transitions.

dryRun.title: onChange: setQuery(v); startTransition(() => setFilter(v))
rows: old transition render is thrown away
dryRun.note: useTransition returns [isPending, startTransition]. State updates inside startTransition are non-urgent. In React 19 the callback may be async (Actions): isPending stays true until the awaited work finishes.

think.q:
function App() {
  const [text, setText] = useState('')
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('')
  const [, startTransition] = useTransition()
  return <><input value={text} onChange={(e) => { setText(e.target.value); startTransition(() => setFilter(e.target.value)) }} /><p>{filter.toUpperCase()}</p></>
}
why: Both updates land in the end; the difference is only priority while work is in progress.

think.q:
function App() {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false)
  const save = () => startTransition(async () => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 20)); startTransition(() => setSaved(true)) })
  return <button onClick={save}>{isPending ? 'saving' : saved ? 'saved' : 'save'}</button>
}
why: React 19 Actions: an async transition keeps isPending true until the awaited work is done. Updates after an await need their own startTransition.

think.q: Why must the input's own value NOT be updated inside startTransition?
opts: A transition can lag behind, so the typed text would appear late or jump
why: Keep the input urgent; move the expensive derived update into the transition.

think.q: Which is a good transition?
opts: Switching to a heavy tab or filtering a large list
why: Transitions are for "can wait a moment" updates.

think.q: How is a transition different from debouncing the filter?
opts: No fixed delay: React starts at once and only drops outdated work; fast devices update immediately
why: Debounce waits even on a fast machine.

try.task: Write a hook useFilteredList(items) returning { query, setQuery, results, isPending }: query updates urgently, results (items containing the query, case-insensitive) are computed from a filter value updated inside a transition.
try.hint: Two states: query and filter. setQuery = (v) => { setQ(v); startTransition(() => setFilter(v)) }; results = useMemo(...).

takeaway.key: useTransition marks updates as non-urgent and gives isPending. Keep input state urgent; React 19 transitions can be async Actions.
mistakes: Putting the input value itself in a transition.

dryRun.title: const deferred = useDeferredValue(query); <Results query={deferred} />
dryRun.note: useDeferredValue(value) gives a copy of a value that lags behind during urgent updates. Use it when you receive the value as a prop (no access to the setter, so no startTransition). Pair it with a memoized child so the deferred render can be skipped or interrupted.

think.q:
function Results({ q }) { return <p>{q}</p> }
function App() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('')
  const d = useDeferredValue(q)
  return <><input value={q} onChange={(e) => setQ(e.target.value)} /><Results q={d} /><i>{String(q !== d)}</i></>
}
why: Once React is idle the deferred value catches up, so it is no longer stale.

think.q: function App() { const d = useDeferredValue('final', 'initial'); return <p>{d}</p> }
why: React 19 accepts an initial value: the first render uses it, then a background render switches to the real value.
think.exec:
import { useState, useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, StrictMode, Fragment, Suspense, useTransition, useDeferredValue, startTransition, use, lazy, forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, Component } from 'react' import { createPortal, flushSync } from 'react-dom' function App() { const d = useDeferredValue('final', 'initial'); return

{d}

} await mount() console.log($('p').textContent)

think.q: When choose useDeferredValue over useTransition?
opts: When you only have the value (e.g. a prop), not the code that sets it
why: Same mechanism, different access point.

think.q: Why wrap the slow child in memo() when using a deferred value?
opts: So renders where the deferred value has not changed can skip the slow child entirely
memo is required by the hook
why: Without memo the slow child re-renders on every urgent render anyway.

think.q: Good way to show results are behind?
why: Users keep seeing useful (slightly old) results.

try.task: Write SearchPage({ items }): an input, and a memoized Results list that receives useDeferredValue(query); the list gets style.opacity = 0.5 while stale (query !== deferred).
examples: while stale the list is dimmed
try.hint: const deferred = useDeferredValue(query); const Results = memo(…); <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.5 : 1 }}>.

takeaway.key: useDeferredValue lets a value lag behind during urgent updates. Combine with memo, show staleness, and use it when you do not own the setter.
mistakes: No memo on the slow child.
Using it for values that must be exact (form submissions).

dryRun.title: <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Profile /><Posts /></Suspense>
dryRun.note: Suspense shows a fallback while something below it is not ready (lazy code, or data read with use()). One boundary = one loading state for everything inside it. Nest boundaries to decide what may appear separately.

think.q:
function cache(fn) { const m = new Map(); return (k) => { if (!m.has(k)) m.set(k, fn(k)); return m.get(k) } }
const wait = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
const getUser = cache(() => wait(100, 'Ada'))
function Name() { return <b>{use(getUser('1'))}</b> }
why: The component suspends on the pending promise, so the fallback shows; then the content replaces it.

think.q:
function cache(fn) { const m = new Map(); return (k) => { if (!m.has(k)) m.set(k, fn(k)); return m.get(k) } }
const wait = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
const fast = cache(() => wait(5, 'header')), slow = cache(() => wait(40, 'posts'))
function H() { return <h1>{use(fast('h'))}</h1> }
function P() { return <p>{use(slow('p'))}</p> }
why: The inner boundary lets the header appear while posts are still loading.

think.q: You switch tabs and the new tab suspends. Without a transition the old tab is replaced by a spinner. With startTransition?
opts: React keeps showing the old tab until the new one is ready (no jarring spinner)
why: Transitions avoid hiding already-visible content.

think.q: Which of these makes a component suspend?
opts: Reading a pending promise with use(), or rendering a lazy() component that has not loaded
why: Effects run after render; they never trigger Suspense.

think.q: A suspended promise rejects. Who handles it?
why: Suspense = loading; error boundary = failure. Use both.

try.task: Write ProfilePage({ userPromise, postsPromise }): shows the user name (from userPromise via use()) under one Suspense boundary ("Loading profile…") and the posts list under a nested boundary ("Loading posts…"), so the name can appear before the posts.
examples: userPromise resolves first → name visible, "Loading posts…" still shown
try.hint: Two small components that call use(promise); ProfilePage wraps them in Suspense boundaries.

takeaway.key: Suspense = declarative loading states. One boundary per independently-loading region; pair with error boundaries; transitions keep old UI instead of flashing spinners.
mistakes: One giant boundary for the whole page.
Expecting useEffect fetches to trigger Suspense.

dryRun.title: use(resource)
rows: throws to the nearest error boundary
like useContext, but allowed inside if/loops
new promise every render → suspends forever (do not)
dryRun.note: use() (React 19) reads a promise or a context. Unlike other hooks it may be called conditionally. Promises must come from outside the render (a cache, a parent, a Server Component, a library), never be created inside the component that reads them.

think.q:
const Theme = createContext('light')
function Label({ show }) { if (!show) return <i>hidden</i>; const t = use(Theme); return <b>{t}</b> }
why: use(Context) works after an early return, which useContext would forbid.

think.q:
const done = Promise.resolve('ready')
function C() { return <b>{use(done)}</b> }
why: A resolved promise just gives its value (after React has seen it settle).
think.exec: import { useState, useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useContext, createContext, memo, StrictMode, Fragment, Suspense, useTransition, useDeferredValue, startTransition, use, lazy, forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, Component } from 'react' import { createPortal, flushSync } from 'react-dom' const done = Promise.resolve('ready') function C() { return {use(done)} } await mount(…}>) await run(() => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 5))) console.log(container.textContent)

think.q: function C() { const data = use(fetch("/api").then((r) => r.json())) }. What happens?
opts: A new promise is created on every render, so it keeps suspending (and refetching)
why: Create or cache the promise outside the component.

think.q: Where do promises for use() often come from in Next.js App Router?
opts: A Server Component starts the fetch and passes the promise to a Client Component
why: The client can render the rest and suspend only where it reads the data.

think.q: How do you handle a rejected promise read with use()?
opts: Wrap the component in an error boundary (try/catch around use() does not work)
why: use() throws to the nearest boundary.

try.task: Write createCache(fetcher) returning read(key) that always returns the SAME promise for a key (safe to pass to use()), plus Comments({ read, postId }) which renders the comment list using use(read(postId)).
try.hint: A Map from key to promise; Comments: const list = use(read(postId)).

checks.t: same key gives the same promise

takeaway.key: use() reads promises (suspends) and context (even conditionally). Promises must be created outside render and cached; errors go to error boundaries.
mistakes: Creating the promise inside the component.

dryRun.title: Next.js App Router page
rows: await db queries, secrets; no state/effects/handlers
dryRun.note: React Server Components (RSC) run only on the server and send rendered output, not their code, to the browser. Mark interactive parts with "use client"; everything imported by that file becomes client code. Push the boundary down to the smallest interactive leaves.

think.q: Which can a Server Component do?
opts: await a database query directly in the component
why: No interactivity or browser APIs on the server.

think.q: You add "use client" to a layout at the top of the app. Consequence?
opts: Everything it imports becomes client code, losing most RSC benefits
why: Keep "use client" on small leaves.

think.q: Which prop can a Server Component pass to a Client Component?
opts: A plain object or array of data (serializable)
why: Functions cannot be serialized (Server Actions are the exception).

think.q: Can a Client Component render a Server Component?
opts: Yes, if the Server Component is passed in as children (or another prop) from a server parent
why: Composition lets server content sit inside client wrappers.

think.q: How are Server Components different from classic SSR?
opts: SSR renders client components to HTML and still ships their JS; RSC never ships the server component's code at all
why: They are often used together.

try.task: Write classifyComponent(info) that decides where a component must run. info: { usesState, usesEffects, hasEventHandlers, usesBrowserApi, readsDatabase, usesSecrets }. Return "client" if it needs interactivity or browser APIs, "server" if it reads a database or secrets (and needs nothing client-side), "conflict" if it needs both (split it), else "either".
try.hint: needsClient = state || effects || handlers || browser API; needsServer = db || secrets.

checks.t: data and secrets stay on the server
both means split it; nothing means either

takeaway.key: Server Components run only on the server (data, secrets, zero JS); "use client" marks interactive leaves. Pass serializable props, compose server content as children.
mistakes: "use client" at the top of the tree.
Passing functions from server to client components.

dryRun.title: renderToPipeableStream(<App />) with a <Suspense> around Comments
rows: hydrates; selective hydration prioritises what the user clicks
React re-renders that part on the client (warning)
dryRun.note: Streaming SSR sends HTML in chunks: the shell first, then each Suspense boundary's content as it is ready. Hydration attaches event handlers to the server HTML; it must match what the client renders first, so no Date.now(), Math.random() or window checks in render.

think.q: Main benefit of streaming over classic renderToString?
opts: The user sees the page shell immediately instead of waiting for the slowest data
why: Slow parts no longer block everything.

think.q: Which render code causes a hydration mismatch?
why: Server and client produce different text. Render the time after mount instead.

think.q: What is selective hydration?
opts: React hydrates Suspense boundaries independently and prioritises the one the user interacts with
why: Clicking a not-yet-hydrated part makes it go first.

think.q: A component must show "Online" from navigator.onLine. How do you avoid a mismatch?
opts: Render a neutral value on the server and in the first client render, then update in an effect (or useSyncExternalStore with getServerSnapshot)
why: The first client render must match the server HTML.

think.q:
import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server'
function Clock() { const [t, setT] = useState(null); useEffect(() => setT('12:00'), []); return <p>{t ?? '--:--'}</p> }
why: Effects do not run on the server, so the HTML has the neutral placeholder; the client fills it in after hydration.
think.exec:
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react' import { renderToString } from 'react-dom/server' function Clock() { const [t, setT] = useState(null); useEffect(() => setT('12:00'), []); return

{t ?? '--:--'}

} console.log(renderToString())

try.task: Write ClientTime({ now }) that is hydration-safe: the server HTML and first client render show "--:--"; after mount it shows now() formatted as HH:MM (24h, from a Date).
try.hint: useState(null); useEffect(() => setTime(now()), [now]); format with padStart.

takeaway.key: Streaming sends the shell first and fills Suspense boundaries as data arrives; hydration must match the server HTML, so render browser-only values after mount.
